description: We are College students passionate about technology, coding, space exploration, and innovation. We aim to participate in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 to learn new things, collaborate, and develop creative solutions to real-world challenges using NASA's open data.
summary:
LunarSpark is a website that tells the life stories of 13 groups of NASA equipment left on the Moon, Mars and in deep space, from Apollo Lunar Modules and Surveyor landers to the Mars rovers, Ingenuity, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer and the Kepler telescope. Each machine has its own page that follows the same path: where it began, what it did, how it worked, what it found, why it was left behind, and where it is now. Pages combine plain-language writing, timelines and NASA photographs, all based on NASA’s mission archives and linked back to NASA.

The site answers the challenge by turning silent hardware into stories anyone can follow. It matters because these machines changed our view of the Moon, Mars and other worlds, and remembering them keeps people curious about exploration.
details:
LunarSpark is a website that tells the stories of 13 groups of NASA equipment left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space: the Apollo Lunar Modules, Lunar Roving Vehicles, ALSEP science stations, Surveyor landers, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, the Viking landers, Phoenix and InSight, Ingenuity, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer and the Kepler telescope.

How it works. Visitors start on an animated home page and choose a destination: the Moon, Mars or deep space. The fleet page lets them filter and search all 13 machines. Each machine has its own page with the same seven chapters: overview, where it began, the mission, how it worked, what it found, why it was left behind and where it is now. Each page also has a key-facts table, a timeline of events, NASA photographs and a link to the NASA source. A separate timeline page shows when each machine last spoke, in order. The aim is that anyone, with no space background, can follow a machine’s life from first design to last signal.

Benefits and impact. The site turns scattered mission records into stories that are easy to read, so people can see that these machines still matter. They gave us the first soil measurements, marsquake recordings, the first powered flight on another planet and thousands of discovered worlds. We hope it makes students and the public more curious about space exploration and shows that spacecraft are worth remembering after they stop working.

Data and resources. All mission facts, text and images come from NASA’s NSSDCA and NASA Science mission pages, as listed in the NASA Data section. Every machine page credits NASA and links to its source page.

Tools. HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, with no frameworks. The animated starfield uses the browser’s canvas. Scroll effects use the browser’s Intersection Observer. We used Claude, an AI assistant, to help write code, organize NASA material into a common page structure and draft summaries and timelines, and we checked the result against NASA’s sources.

Creativity. The design feels like a night-sky archive. It has a glowing moon, radar-style pings for the last signal received from each machine, a live ticker of those last signals, animated counters and cards that tilt as you move over them.

What we considered. We wanted clear, accurate stories, so every page follows the same structure and points back to NASA. We also made it work on phones and for visitors who prefer less motion.
